title: Samson (Judges 13–16)
hook: great strength, poor choices, and one last prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's fleece, and an army cut down to three hundred. Your line was fewer is enough. What did you start with less? Day three hundred ninety-four.

A few days before Christmas, the weekday Mass reading sounds almost like a Gospel. A woman who has never been able to have children is visited by a messenger of God. You will conceive and bear a son, he tells her, and no razor will touch his head. He'll be set apart for God from his mother's womb. That child grows up astonishingly strong. He tears a lion apart with his hands. He carries off a city's gates. And he makes one wrong choice after another. His name is Samson.
screen: `A READING BEFORE CHRISTMAS.` → `NO RAZOR SHALL TOUCH HIS HEAD.` → `STRONG, AND CHOOSING BADLY.`

segments.voice: Samson is a Nazarite, spelled Nazirite in other English Bibles: someone consecrated to God, who drinks no wine and never cuts his hair. The long hair is the sign of the vow. The strength is God's gift. Keep those two apart, because Samson doesn't. He marries outside his people against his parents' pleading. He sets three hundred foxes loose with torches in the enemy's fields. He's ruled by appetite and revenge, and the text tells it straight, without excuse. Then Delilah. Three times she asks what makes him strong, three times he lies, and three times the Philistines burst in. The fourth time he tells her the truth, in the Douay-Rheims: "if my head be shaven, my strength shall depart from me." She lulls him to sleep on her knees, calls a barber, and his seven locks are shaved. Then comes the line that matters most. He wakes and thinks he'll shake himself free as before, "not knowing that the Lord was departed from him." The hair wasn't magic. Some readers see it as the last piece of a vow he had been bending all along. Blinded and chained, he grinds grain in a prison. His hair starts to grow. At a feast for their god, they bring him out to mock him, and he prays: "O Lord God, remember me, and restore to me now my former strength." The text doesn't hide that the rest of the prayer asks for revenge for his eyes. He pushes the pillars, and the house falls on him and on them. The Church doesn't hold Samson up as a model of virtue. But the Letter to the Hebrews names him among the people of faith. Strength never made Samson wise. At the end, it was a prayer that made him remember who his strength belonged to.
screen: `A NAZARITE: SET APART FOR GOD.` · `STRONG, AND RULED BY APPETITE.` · `THE LORD WAS DEPARTED FROM HIM.` · `REMEMBER ME, O LORD GOD.` · then, large: `RESTORE TO ME NOW MY FORMER STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your weakness. Settle, and breathe. Samson's trouble wasn't a lack of strength. It was a soft spot he kept walking back into: flattery, anger, wanting what he wanted. Name yours, quietly, to yourself. The thing that gets past your guard every time. Don't argue with it. Just look at it the way you'd look at a door you keep leaving unlocked. If you pray, you can borrow Samson's words: O Lord God, remember me. If you don't, simply let yourself be seen, by yourself, without excuses. The bell holds the time.
Samson. A judge consecrated to God from the womb, given great strength, who ruined much of it, and whose last act was a prayer. Today's word.
Your line: strength isn't wisdom. Today, when you feel most sure of yourself, pause one breath before you act. Day three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the announcement of Samson's birth at daily Mass in late Advent, paired with the angel's announcement of John the Baptist's birth, and the Church reads his life as a warning as much as an example.

fork.setup: you're Samson. blind, chained, mocked at your enemies' feast, your hair just beginning to grow back. what do you do?
options: call on God to remember you.
fork.reveal: he prays, "O Lord God, remember me," and pulls down the pillars. after a life of bad choices, his last act begins with a prayer.

original.note: Hebrew: nazir, the name for one under the vow. The vow is laid out in Numbers 6.

trapdoor: what you thought: Samson's strength was in his hair.
what it means: the hair was the sign of his vow to God. when the last sign of the vow was gone, the text says the Lord had departed from him.
what a scholar hears: the vow in Numbers 6 runs for a set number of days; Samson's, the angel says, runs from the womb to the day of his death.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'strongest man in the Bible' and 'almost every wrong choice' (superlatives); 'most English Bibles' cut; the barber line follows the Douay's ambiguity (she calls a barber; the locks are shaved); 'a promise he'd been breaking for years' made 'some readers see'; added that 16:28 goes on to ask for revenge; replaced the Douay haircut myth item; cut the nazir root etymology; added the Lectionary as a source.
Advent reading: Judges 13:2–7, 24–25 is read at Mass on December 19 with Luke 1:5–25. Confirm in the current Lectionary.
Samson's foxes (Judges 15:4–5), lion (14:6) and the gates of Gaza (16:3) are summarized; confirm.
